name: Bowsprit Reach
geological_features: An elongated body nearly three times longer than it is wide
Parallel grooves running the length of the body suggesting ancient stress fractures
A pronounced rocky promontory at the leading orbital edge
description: Bowsprit Reach is an oddly elongated rocky body whose shape resembles a ship's bowsprit thrusting forward through the void. The planetoid measures nearly twelve thousand kilometers along its long axis but only four thousand across, a cigar-shaped mass of iron-rich stone that tumbles end over end in a slow, majestic rotation. The leading edge sports a pronounced rocky promontory that gives the body its nautical name, a spear of stone pointing perpetually in the direction of orbital travel.

The surface is grey and pitted, scored with parallel grooves that run the entire length of the body like the grain in a piece of cosmic driftwood. These grooves are believed to be stress fractures from the impact that gave Bowsprit Reach its elongated shape, frozen in stone when the material cooled and solidified. Without atmosphere, the grooves remain sharp-edged after billions of years, their shadows creating a striking striped pattern visible from orbit.

Bowsprit Reach's unusual shape has made it a useful navigational reference point in a system otherwise lacking distinctive landmarks. Its tumbling rotation is precisely predictable and has been used to calibrate sensor arrays and navigation computers. Some pilot traditions hold that passing close to the bowsprit brings good luck on a voyage, a superstition that has resulted in at least two recorded near-collisions by crews taking the tradition too literally.

A small automated relay station clings to the promontory tip, taking advantage of the rotation to sweep its signal across a wide arc of space with each tumble. Mining surveys have confirmed modest iron and silicon deposits throughout the body, but the awkward shape and rotation make extraction impractical for all but the most desperate operators. Bowsprit Reach remains what it has always been — a landmark, a curiosity, and a navigator's friend.
